prompt: The shop is starting a new serverless Python function app in 2026. Which plan does Microsoft's documentation point it to?

choices.text: The Consumption plan, on Linux
choices.why: Linux Consumption is marked retired in the hosting table, gets no new language versions, and the option retires on 30 September 2028.

choices.text: The Flex Consumption plan
choices.why: The documentation calls it the recommended serverless plan, and Python runs only on Linux, where it is the serverless option left.

choices.text: The Consumption plan, on Windows
choices.why: Windows Consumption is still available, but Python is not supported on Windows in Azure Functions.

choices.text: A Premium plan with no always ready instances
choices.why: A Premium plan always has at least one billed instance, so it is never serverless in the pay-per-execution sense.

prompt: Match each plan with what it charges for, as the documentation describes it.

pairs.right: executions and memory while executing, plus any always ready instances
the cores and memory of every allocated instance, with no execution charge
the App Service plan, however many apps it holds
executions, and memory times execution time, with nothing kept ready

right_distractors: each request's CPU time, whatever the memory

prompt: `take_order` sits on a Flex Consumption app whose timeout in `host.json` is unbounded. A customer's order takes six minutes to price. What does the customer get?

choices.text: The answer after six minutes, since nothing bounds the timeout
choices.why: The function may keep running, but the caller is behind a load balancer whose idle timeout is 230 seconds.

choices.text: No answer: an HTTP function has 230 seconds, whatever the timeout says
choices.why: The documentation gives 230 seconds as the most an HTTP-triggered function can take to respond, because of the load balancer in front.

choices.text: A refusal when the app starts, because unbounded is not allowed on Flex
choices.why: Unbounded is allowed on Flex Consumption; the limit that bites here is the HTTP one.

choices.text: The answer after five minutes, the Consumption default
choices.why: Five minutes is the legacy Consumption plan's default; this app is on Flex, whose default is 30.

prompt: `flex.bicep` compiled with no warning at `instanceMemoryMB: 1024` and `maximumInstanceCount: 2000`. Which of these does that tell you? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The resource types call both properties a number, and both values are numbers
choices.why: That is all the compiler checks here: the type, not which numbers the service offers.

choices.text: Azure offers 1,024 MB instances on Flex Consumption
choices.why: The documentation lists 512, 2,048 and 4,096 MB; the compiler did not ask.

choices.text: Whether Azure accepts the file is still unknown on the laptop
choices.why: Only the service answers that, and nothing here sent it the template.

choices.text: The ceiling of 1,000 instances applies only to Premium
choices.why: 1,000 is Flex Consumption's own most per function group; the compiler simply does not know it.

choices.text: A clean compile is not proof the values are allowed
choices.why: The documentation rules out both values, and the compiler passed them anyway.

prompt: On Flex Consumption, a burst of receipts piles up on the `orders` queue. What happens to the instances answering `take_order`?

choices.text: They stay as they are: `make_receipt` scales on instances of its own
choices.why: Flex scales each function on its own except the HTTP, Event Grid blob and Durable groups, so the queue function gets separate instances.

choices.text: They grow too, because every function in an app scales together
choices.why: That is how Consumption and Premium scale, per app; Flex scales per function.

choices.text: They are shared with `make_receipt` until the HTTP group is full
choices.why: The HTTP group holds HTTP functions only; a queue trigger is in a group of its own.

choices.text: They shrink, to free the regional quota for the queue
choices.why: The regional quota limits the total; it does not take instances from one group to give to another.

prompt: Put in order what a cold request to `take_order` waits for, from the first step to the answer.
items: The platform finds an instance and gives it the app
The Functions host starts and reads `host.json`
The host starts the Python worker
The host hands the request to `take_order`
trap: Putting the import before the worker: the file is imported by the worker, so the worker has to exist first.

prompt: On the legacy Consumption plan a request lands on a prewarmed placeholder. What does it still wait for?

choices.text: Nothing: a placeholder is an instance kept ready for the app
choices.why: A placeholder is generic; it becomes your app only when the request arrives, so your file is not loaded yet.

choices.text: The host and the worker starting, as on any cold start
choices.why: Those are exactly what the placeholder has running already, by the documentation's description.

choices.text: The import of `function_app.py`, and then the call
choices.why: The host and the worker are running, but the placeholder could not have known your file, so the import is still paid.

choices.text: Only the package download, because Consumption has no worker
choices.why: Every plan runs a language worker beside the host; the placeholder has one started.

prompt: On a Premium plan, one function of the app is called on each new instance during scale-out, before the instance takes traffic, to open connections early. Its trigger is the ___ trigger.
The shop puts the nightly sales report in the same function app as `take_order`, and the report imports a large data library at the top of `function_app.py`. Who pays for that import?

choices.text: Only the report, once a night when its timer fires
choices.why: The import runs when the worker loads the file, on every new instance, whichever function the instance is for.

choices.text: Every cold start of the app, `take_order`'s included
choices.why: One app is one file imported once per instance, so the order API's cold starts carry the report's library.

choices.text: Nobody, because Flex Consumption imports each function separately
choices.why: Flex scales functions on separate instances, but each instance still imports the whole `function_app.py`.

choices.text: Only warm requests, which re-import the library each time
choices.why: Python keeps a module once imported; the cost is at the import, which is the cold start.

prompt: Microsoft's guidance says to create clients at module level in Python. What does that do to the cold start?

choices.text: Shortens it, because the client is built before the instance exists
choices.why: Module level runs during the import, on the instance; it is part of the cold start.

choices.text: Lengthens it a little, so that every warm call reuses the client
choices.why: The client is built once at the import, and each warm request uses the connection instead of opening one.

choices.text: Nothing, since clients are built by the host and not by the worker
choices.why: A client your code builds is your code's; only bindings are the host's.

choices.text: Removes it, because a module-level client keeps the instance warm
choices.why: Nothing in your code decides whether the platform keeps an instance; that is the plan's.

prompt: `first200` counted about forty `000` codes before the first `200`. What does `000` mean there?

choices.text: No HTTP answer at all: nothing listened on 7071 yet
choices.why: `000` is `curl`'s code for no HTTP answer; nothing listened on 7071 until the host was ready.

choices.text: The function ran and returned an empty body
choices.why: A function that ran would give a real status, 200 or 500; `000` is no answer at all.

choices.text: The host answered that it was still starting
choices.why: A host answering would send a real HTTP status; on the laptop it sent nothing until it was ready.

choices.text: Azurite refused the host's storage connection
choices.why: That would show in the host's log, not as `curl`'s status for a request to the app.

prompt: Why does each run of `first200` begin with `docker rm -f cold`?

choices.text: To clear Azurite's lease, which would otherwise block the host
choices.why: The lease is in Azurite, which keeps running; each new container takes a lease of its own.

choices.text: So each run starts with no instance at all: a cold start
choices.why: A container that is already running is a warm instance; removing it makes the next `docker run` a start from nothing.

choices.text: Because Docker cannot publish port 7071 twice in one minute
choices.why: The port is freed when the container is removed; there is no wait. Two running containers are what would collide.

choices.text: To delete the image, so the build is measured too
choices.why: `docker rm` removes a container, not an image; the build is done once, before the runs.

prompt: `shopfn:slow` sleeps for 8 seconds at import. In the laptop's log, the start script's first line came 12.43 s before `Initializing Host`, against 5.09 s for `shopfn:1`. How many seconds longer is that, to two decimals?
hint: A little less than the sleep: part of a short import hides behind the host's own start.

prompt: With `--cpus 0.25`, the same image took about three times as long to its first 200 as with a whole processor. What does that suggest about a 512 MB Flex Consumption instance?

choices.text: Nothing, because Flex gives every size the same processor
choices.why: The documentation pairs 512 MB with a quarter of a core and 2,048 MB with one; memory and processor come together.

choices.text: A longer cold start, since it gets a quarter of a core
choices.why: Starting the host is computation, and the laptop's analogue slowed as the processor shrank; Azure's own figure was not measured.

choices.text: It will be refused for Python, which needs a whole core
choices.why: Nothing in the documentation ties Python to a size; all three are offered.

choices.text: Its cold start is three times as long in Azure, exactly
choices.why: The laptop's ratio is the laptop's; it suggests a direction, not Azure's number.

prompt: In the timestamped log, about five seconds pass between the start script's first line and `Initializing Host`. Which of these is it fair to conclude?

choices.text: Azure's cold start for this app is about five seconds
choices.why: These are the laptop's numbers; Azure's platform steps, and its placeholders, were not measured.

choices.text: The function itself is slow, and should be rewritten
choices.why: Once ready, `take_order` answered in milliseconds; the seconds are spent before any function runs.

choices.text: On the laptop, most of the wait comes before the host logs anything about the app
choices.why: The function's own time is small next to it; that is the shape the laptop shows, and only the shape transfers.

choices.text: Azurite is slow to answer, and a real storage account would remove it
choices.why: Nothing in the log points at storage; the gap is before the host has initialised at all.

prompt: With `plans.py`'s illustrative rates, one order on a 2 GB instance billed for 1 second costs 0.0000524 USD. How many orders a month cost the same as the always-on instance at 150 USD? Round to the nearest thousand.
Keep `plans.py`'s rates, but put the order API on a 512 MB instance, which is 0.5 GB, still billed 1 second an order. What does one order cost, in USD?
hint: 0.5 GB × 1 s × 0.000026, plus the execution's share of 0.40 per million.

prompt: The shop's order API takes about 400,000 orders a month, roughly 0.15 a second, mostly in the daytime. With `plans.py`'s illustrative rates, what does keeping one instance always on buy it?

choices.text: A lower bill, since the shop is above the break-even
choices.why: The break-even is about 1.09 a second; at 0.15 a second, on demand costs about 21 USD against 150.

choices.text: Nothing at all: on demand already has no cold start at this rate
choices.why: At night the app goes idle for minutes at a time, and the next order meets a cold start.

choices.text: The end of the morning's cold starts, for most of the 150 USD
choices.why: On demand costs about 21 USD here, so the instance is roughly 129 USD a month spent on latency, not saved.

choices.text: A higher limit on instances, which on demand caps at one
choices.why: On-demand Flex scales out to its maximum instance count, 100 by default; nothing caps it at one.

prompt: Microsoft's cost example runs 40 requests a second, 10 at a time, on 2 GB Flex instances. Why is the IO-bound case about 0.25 USD an hour and the CPU-bound one about 1.93?

choices.text: CPU time is billed on Flex and waiting is not
choices.why: The documentation bills memory while an instance executes; CPU does not appear in the meter.

choices.text: The CPU-bound app pays a higher rate per GB-second
choices.why: Both cases use the same assumed rate, 0.000026 per GB-second.

choices.text: The IO-bound requests are fewer, so fewer executions are billed
choices.why: Both run the same 144,000 executions an hour, 0.0576 USD of the total.

choices.text: Ten requests share one active instance instead of keeping ten active
choices.why: The meter counts the memory of active instances, so one busy instance costs a tenth of ten busy ones for the same work.

prompt: Suppose the free grant were 100,000 GB-s a month, a number invented for this question. With 2 GB billed for 1 second an order, by how many orders a month does the grant move the break-even up?
hint: Each order uses 2 GB-s of the grant before it costs anything.

prompt: Which plan answers a request with no cold start and also scales to zero when nobody calls?

choices.text: Premium, with its prewarmed instances
choices.why: Premium always keeps at least one billed instance; it never scales to zero.

choices.text: Dedicated, with Always On
choices.why: Always On keeps the host running on the plan's instances, which is the opposite of scaling to zero.

choices.text: Flex Consumption, with one always ready instance per group
choices.why: An always ready instance is never taken away, so the group does not go to zero while it has one.

choices.text: None of them: an instance kept ready is an instance kept
choices.why: Removing the cold start means something is running before the request, and that is what scaling to zero gives up.

prompt: Match each setting with the plan it belongs to.
A plan named `P1V2` scales by hand or by autoscale rules and never on events, because despite its letter it is not Elastic Premium but a ___ plan.
The finance export runs once a night, is triggered from a queue, and takes four minutes. On demand, at `plans.py`'s rates, what is the case for paying for an always-on instance for it?

choices.text: Its cold start delays a customer, so readiness is worth the price
choices.why: A queue trigger has nobody waiting; a few seconds of start add a few seconds to a file read in the morning.

choices.text: It runs longer than the five-minute limit and needs Premium
choices.why: Four minutes is under every plan's default, and Flex's default is 30 minutes anyway.

choices.text: Hardly any: nobody waits, and it bills minutes a night
choices.why: Four minutes of a 2 GB instance is about 0.012 USD a night at these rates; readiness buys nothing anyone sees.

choices.text: On demand cannot run a queue trigger without one instance kept
choices.why: Flex scales queue triggers from zero on events; nothing needs to be kept.
